title: Why did you choose microservices instead of a modular monolith?
description: Learn to explain the trade-offs between microservices and a modular monolith, when each makes sense, and how to defend your architecture decision in an interview.

data.text: When an interviewer asks why you chose microservices over a modular monolith, they are really testing whether you understand architectural trade-offs. The honest answer is usually: it depends. A modular monolith is often the better starting point, and microservices introduce complexity you should only pay for when you have a clear need.

A modular monolith is a single deployable application with clear internal boundaries between modules. Each module owns its data and exposes a well-defined interface to other modules. Everything runs in one process, shares the same database (ideally with schema separation), and is deployed together.

data.title: Advantages
items: Simple deployment and local development—one project, one database
Strong consistency across modules in a single transaction

data.title: Disadvantages
items: Scaling is coarse-grained—you must scale the whole app
Technology choices are shared across the team
A bug in one module can destabilize the entire process
Long-term enforcement of module boundaries requires discipline

data.title: Interview framing
data.text: Start by acknowledging that both architectures can work. Explain the specific pressures—team size, deployment frequency, failure isolation—that made microservices the right choice for your situation.

data.title: Team context drives the decision
data.content: A two-person startup building a SaaS product should start with a modular monolith. When the same company grows to ten teams across three continents, they may extract billing, notifications, and search into separate services. The architecture evolved with the need, not the other way around.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Start with a modular monolith unless you have a proven need for microservices
Microservices trade operational simplicity for independent scaling and team autonomy
The right choice depends on team size, deployment frequency, and failure isolation needs
